lesson.child_mission: Australian coins and notes have dollar or cent values. Count money by grouping same values and converting 100 cents to 1 dollar.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Total: two $2 coins, one $1, three 20c. Write dollars and cents.

FEEDBACK
$2+$2+$1+60c = $5.60.

WATCH FOR
Adding coin counts without using their values (counting "five coins" as $5) ignores denominations.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Make eight money collections with coins/notes (draw or list). Find each total in dollars and cents. Include at least two that require regrouping cents into dollars.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Three $1 coins and two 50c coins total $3 + $1 = $4 (because 50c+50c=$1). A $5 note and a $2 coin total $7.

TRY FIRST
Total: two $2 coins, one $1, three 20c. Write dollars and cents.

FEEDBACK
$2+$2+$1+60c = $5.60.
teach_steps.explain:
Australian coins and notes have dollar or cent values. Count money by grouping same values and converting 100 cents to 1 dollar.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Adding coin counts without using their values (counting "five coins" as $5) ignores denominations. Correct the value or method, not just the appearance of the digits.
